fields.title: Joel
fields.subtitle: Yoel, “The LORD is God”
fields.description: A short, urgent book that begins with a plague of locusts stripping the land bare and hears in it the coming day of the LORD. Joel calls priests and farmers, elders and children to a holy fast — “Tear your hearts, not your clothes” — and in answer God sends back the rain, promises to make up for the years the locust has eaten, and makes the promise Peter quoted at Pentecost: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all people.” It ends in the valley of decision, with the LORD roaring from Zion and a spring flowing from his house. Set out line by line as the poetry it is, in the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Joel?
qa.answer: The second of the twelve shorter prophetic books of the Old Testament, three chapters long in English Bibles. It begins with a devastating plague of locusts, calls the people to fast and return to the LORD, and turns at 2:18 from lament to promise: rain and harvest restored, the Spirit poured out on all people, the nations judged, and the LORD dwelling in Zion. Its great theme is the day of the LORD, the day when God acts to judge and to save.

qa.question: Who wrote the book of Joel, and when?
qa.answer: The book opens, “The LORD’s word came to Joel son of Pethuel” (1:1), and nothing more is known of him. Unlike most prophets he names no king, so his date is uncertain. Some scholars place him early, in the ninth century BC; many place him after the return from exile in Babylon, perhaps around 400 BC, pointing to the role of elders and priests and the mention of the Greeks (3:6); others date him in between. The book’s message does not depend on the answer.

qa.question: What is the day of the LORD in Joel?
qa.answer: The day when God intervenes in history to judge evil and rescue his people. Joel sees a foretaste of it in the locust plague (“the day of the LORD is close at hand”, 1:15) and warns that it is first a day of darkness for Judah itself, “great and very terrible” (2:11). But for those who return to him it becomes a day of rescue: “all who call on the name of the LORD will be saved” (2:32). In chapter 3 it is the day when the nations are judged in the valley of decision.

qa.question: Is the army in Joel 2 locusts or soldiers?
qa.answer: Readers have answered in different ways. Some think chapter 2 describes the same locust plague as chapter 1, pictured as an invading army; others think it is a human army, perhaps the “northern army” of 2:20, of which the locusts were a warning; others see in it the hosts of the final day of the LORD. Joel himself calls the locusts God’s “great army” (2:25), and the poem may hold all three together, the present disaster opening a window onto the last one.

qa.question: How is Joel connected with Pentecost?
qa.answer: On the day of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit came on the first disciples and they spoke in other languages, Peter told the crowd, “this is what was spoken through the prophet Joel” (Acts 2:16), and quoted Joel 2:28–32: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all people. Your sons and your daughters will prophesy”. Paul quotes its last line, that all who call on the name of the Lord will be saved, in Romans 10:13. Christians read the promise as fulfilled in the gift of the Spirit to the whole church.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Tear your hearts, not your clothes, and turn back to the LORD your God, for he is gracious and full of tender compassion, slow to grow angry and rich in loyal love, and he relents from sending disaster.

— Joel 2:13

Joel begins with a disaster everyone could see. A plague of locusts has swept over the land, wave after wave, and stripped it bare: the vines, the fig trees, the grain, the very bark of the trees. There is nothing left to offer in the temple, and the farmers and the priests are in mourning together. Out of that ruined landscape the prophet hears God speak, and what he hears runs from the next harvest all the way to the end of history.

The book is only three chapters long, yet the church has never stopped quoting it. On the day of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit came on the disciples, Peter stood up and explained what the crowd was seeing in Joel’s words: “No, this is what was spoken through the prophet Joel”.

A land stripped bare

The first chapter is a call to lament. Joel summons the elders, the drunkards, the farmers, the vine growers and the priests, and asks whether anything like this has happened in their lifetime or their ancestors’. He names the plague four times over:

What the cutting locust left, the swarming locust has eaten. What the swarming locust left, the hopping locust has eaten, and what the hopping locust left, the stripping locust has eaten.

— Joel 1:4

The four names may be stages in the locust’s life or simply four words for the same devouring swarm; either way the effect is total. Joel describes it as an invasion: “For a nation has invaded my land, powerful and too many to count. Its teeth are a lion’s teeth”. And he tells the priests what to do with their grief: “Proclaim a holy fast; call a solemn assembly”, and gather everyone at the house of the LORD to cry to him for help.

Then, for the first time, Joel names what this disaster is a foretaste of: “For the day of the LORD is close at hand, and it will come like ruin from the Almighty.”

The day of the LORD

The day of the LORD is Joel’s great theme. It means the day when God steps in to put the world right, the day of his judgment and his rescue. Many in Israel looked forward to it as a day of victory over their enemies. Joel, like Amos before or after him, warns that it is first a day of reckoning for God’s own people.

Chapter 2 opens with a trumpet in Zion and a vision of an army sweeping in like the dawn across the mountains. They look like horses and charge like warriors; they climb the walls and come in through the windows like a thief; before them the land is “like the garden of Eden”, behind them “a desolate wilderness”. And at their head is the LORD himself:

The LORD thunders at the head of his army; his forces are vast, and mighty is the one who carries out his command. The day of the LORD is great and very terrible. Who can endure it?

— Joel 2:11

Readers differ over what this army is. Some take it as the same locust plague described again as an army; others as a human army, perhaps from the north, of which the locusts were a warning; others as the hosts of the final day itself, painted in the colours of the locusts. The poem may be all three at once, the present disaster opening a window onto the last one.

“Yet even now”

Then, at the darkest point, the tone changes:

Yet even now, declares the LORD, turn back to me with all your heart, with fasting and weeping and mourning.

— Joel 2:12

Joel asks for tears and fasting, but he will not let them become a performance: “Tear your hearts, not your clothes”. The reason he gives for hope is the description of God that the LORD proclaimed to Moses on Mount Sinai: gracious, full of compassion, slow to anger, rich in loyal love. Jonah quotes the same words, with very different feelings. And Joel adds a humble “Who knows? He may turn back and relent”. He does not presume on God’s mercy; he simply throws himself on it.

Everyone is to come, the elders and the children and the nursing babies, even the bride and bridegroom from their wedding chamber. The priests are to weep between the porch and the altar and pray that God’s people not become a byword among the nations, who would ask, “Where is their God?”

The years the locust has eaten

And God answers. “Then the LORD became jealous for his land and took pity on his people.” The rain returns; the threshing floors are heaped with grain; the fig tree and the vine give their fruit. And God makes a promise that has comforted people in every kind of loss:

I will make up to you for the years that the swarming locust has eaten, the hopping locust, the stripping locust, and the cutting locust, my great army that I sent against you.

— Joel 2:25

He calls the locusts “my great army”. Even the disaster was in his hand, and so is the restoring. Twice he says, “Never again will my people be put to shame.”

“I will pour out my Spirit”

Then the promise widens from rain on the fields to something far greater:

And afterward I will pour out my Spirit upon all people. Your sons and your daughters will prophesy; your old men will have dreams, and your young men will see visions. Even on servants, men and women alike, in those days I will pour out my Spirit.

— Joel 2:28–29

In Israel the Spirit of the LORD had come on chosen people for particular tasks: prophets, judges, kings. Joel foresees a day when he will be given to everyone, young and old, men and women, even the servants. Moses had once wished that all the LORD’s people were prophets; Joel says the day is coming. Peter announced at Pentecost that it had come, and Paul, quoting the line that follows, applied it to Jew and Gentile alike: “all who call on the name of the Lord will be saved.”

The valley of decision

The last chapter gathers the nations into “the valley of Jehoshaphat”, a name that means “the LORD judges”, to answer for what they have done to God’s people: scattering them, dividing their land, selling their children for wine. In a bitter reversal of the words of Isaiah and Micah, the nations are told to “Hammer your plow blades into swords” and come to battle. But the battle is a harvest, and it is God’s:

Crowds upon crowds in the valley of decision! Yes, the day of the LORD is close at hand in the valley of decision.

— Joel 3:14

Joel’s “valley of decision” is often preached as the place where each of us must decide for God. In the book it is the place where God decides, giving his verdict on the nations. Yet the two readings are not far apart, for the call to turn back to him with all your heart comes before that verdict is given.

The book ends with the LORD roaring from Zion, mountains dripping with sweet wine, and a spring flowing out from the house of the LORD to water the dry valleys. The land stripped bare in chapter 1 becomes a garden, and its last words are a promise of presence: “The LORD dwells in Zion.”

How to read Joel

Read Joel in one sitting; it takes about fifteen minutes. Notice how it turns in the middle, at 2:18, from lament and warning to promise.

The book does not say when Joel lived. It names no king, and speaks of elders and priests, of the temple and its offerings, and of Judah’s people sold to the Greeks. Some scholars date it early, in the ninth century before Christ; many date it after the return from exile in Babylon, perhaps around 400 BC; others place it in between. Its message does not depend on the date. It speaks to any people who have seen their world stripped bare and wonder whether God is still there.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. Joel is poetry throughout, and this edition prints each line on its own, as the Hebrew sets it out. Where the Hebrew uses God’s personal name, it writes “the LORD”. The Hebrew word hesed is translated “loyal love”: God is “rich in loyal love”. The four locusts of 1:4 are named, as in the Hebrew, “the cutting locust”, “the swarming locust”, “the hopping locust” and “the stripping locust”.

The Hebrew divides Joel into four chapters, beginning a new one at the promise of the Spirit. This edition follows the three chapters of English Bibles, and the references in it follow the English numbering. For the reasoning behind every sentence, with the Hebrew beside it, see openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Joel 1
fields.body_html:
The locusts and the ruined land

1The LORD’s word came to Joel son of Pethuel.
2Hear this, you elders!
Listen, all who live in the land!
Has anything like this happened in your days,
or in the days of your ancestors?
3Tell your children about it,
and let your children tell their children,
and their children the generation after them.
4What the cutting locust left, the swarming locust has eaten.
What the swarming locust left, the hopping locust has eaten,
and what the hopping locust left, the stripping locust has eaten.
5Wake up, you drunkards, and weep!
Wail, all you who drink wine,
because the sweet wine has been cut off from your lips.
6For a nation has invaded my land,
powerful and too many to count.
Its teeth are a lion’s teeth;
it has the fangs of a lioness.
7It has laid waste my vines
and turned my fig trees to broken stumps.
It has stripped off their bark and thrown it down,
and their branches are left white.
8Mourn like a young woman dressed in sackcloth,
grieving for the man she was pledged to marry.
9Grain offerings and drink offerings have ceased in the house of the LORD.
The priests grieve,
those who serve the LORD.
10The fields are laid waste; the ground is in mourning,
for the grain is ruined,
the new wine has dried up, and the olive oil has failed.
11Be dismayed, you farmers! Wail, you who tend the vines,
over the wheat and the barley,
because the harvest of the field is lost.
12The vine has withered,
the fig tree droops;
pomegranate, palm, and apple tree, all the trees of the field are dried up.
Surely joy has withered away from the people.

A call to fast and cry out to the LORD

13Put on sackcloth and mourn, you priests!
Wail, you who serve at the altar!
Come, spend the night in sackcloth, you who serve my God!
For grain offerings and drink offerings are kept back from the house of your God.
14Proclaim a holy fast; call a solemn assembly.
Gather the elders and all who live in the land
at the house of the LORD your God,
and cry to the LORD for help.
15Alas for that day!
For the day of the LORD is close at hand,
and it will come like ruin from the Almighty.
16Has not the food been cut off before our very eyes,
and joy and gladness from the house of our God?
17The seeds lie shriveled under the clods;
the storehouses stand empty;
the granaries are falling down,
for the grain has withered.
18How the animals moan! The herds of cattle wander about in confusion,
because they have no pasture;
the flocks of sheep are suffering as well.
19To you, LORD, I cry out,
for fire has devoured the pastures in the wilderness,
and flames have burned up all the trees of the field.
20Even the wild animals long for you,
because the streams of water have dried up,
and fire has devoured the pastures in the wilderness.
fields.summary: A plague of locusts has devastated the land, and Joel calls the elders, the drinkers and the priests to mourn and to cry out to God.

fields.title: Joel 2
fields.body_html:
The day of the LORD and its army

1Blow the ram’s horn in Zion!
Sound the battle alarm on my holy mountain!
Let everyone who lives in the land tremble,
for the day of the LORD is on its way; it is close at hand.
2It is a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and deep darkness.
Like the dawn spreading across the mountains
comes a great and mighty people.
Nothing like it has ever been before,
and nothing like it will ever be again
through all the generations to come.
3Fire devours in front of them,
and behind them a flame blazes.
Ahead of them the land is like the garden of Eden; behind them it is a desolate wilderness;
nothing escapes them.
4They look like horses;
like war horses they charge.
5With a noise like chariots they leap over the mountaintops,
like the crackling of a blazing fire that burns up stubble,
like a mighty army lined up for battle.
6At the sight of them nations writhe in anguish;
every face turns pale.
7They charge like warriors;
they scale the wall like soldiers.
Each one marches straight ahead;
none of them breaks rank.
8They do not push one another;
each marches in its own track.
They plunge through the weapons and do not stop.
9They swarm over the city; they run along the wall;
they climb into the houses;
they come in through the windows like a thief.
10Before them the earth quakes
and the sky shakes;
the sun and moon go dark,
and the stars lose their brightness.
11The LORD thunders at the head of his army;
his forces are vast,
and mighty is the one who carries out his command.
The day of the LORD is great and very terrible. Who can endure it?
12Yet even now, declares the LORD,
turn back to me with all your heart,
with fasting and weeping and mourning.
13Tear your hearts, not your clothes,
and turn back to the LORD your God,
for he is gracious and full of tender compassion,
slow to grow angry and rich in loyal love,
and he relents from sending disaster.
14Who knows? He may turn back and relent,
and leave behind him a blessing:
grain offerings and drink offerings
for the LORD your God.

The people gather, and the LORD answers

15Blow the ram’s horn in Zion!
Proclaim a holy fast; call a solemn assembly.
16Gather the people; make the assembly holy; bring together the elders;
gather the children,
even babies nursing at the breast.
Let the bridegroom leave his own room
and the bride her wedding chamber.
17Between the porch and the altar
let the priests weep,
those who serve the LORD.
Let them pray, “Have pity on your people, LORD! Do not let your inheritance become a disgrace, a byword among the nations.
Why should the peoples be allowed to say,
‘Where is their God?’”
18Then the LORD became jealous for his land
and took pity on his people.
19The LORD answered his people and said: I am sending you grain, new wine, and olive oil,
and you will have all you want.
Never again will I make you a disgrace among the nations.
20I will drive the northern army far away from you, into a dry and desolate land,
its vanguard into the eastern sea,
and its rear into the western sea.
Its stench will rise; its rotting smell will go up,
for it has done great harm.
21Do not be afraid, O land!
Be glad and rejoice,
for the LORD has done great things!
22Do not be afraid, you wild animals,
for the pastures in the wilderness are turning green.
The trees are bearing their fruit;
the fig tree and the vine give their full yield.
23People of Zion, be glad; rejoice in the LORD your God!
He has given you the autumn rain in his faithfulness.
He has poured down rain for you, the autumn rain and the spring rain, as before.
24The threshing floors will be heaped with grain;
the vats will overflow with new wine and olive oil.
25I will make up to you for the years
that the swarming locust has eaten,
the hopping locust, the stripping locust, and the cutting locust,
my great army
that I sent against you.
26You will eat your fill and be satisfied,
and you will praise the name of the LORD your God,
the one who has worked wonders for you.
Never again will my people be put to shame.
27Then you will know that I am in the midst of Israel,
that I, the LORD, am your God, and there is no other.
Never again will my people be put to shame.

28And afterward I will pour out my Spirit upon all people.
Your sons and your daughters will prophesy;
your old men will have dreams,
and your young men will see visions.
29Even on servants, men and women alike,
in those days
I will pour out my Spirit.
30I will show wonders
in the sky and on the earth:
blood and fire
and columns of smoke.
31The sun will turn dark
and the moon blood red
before the day of the LORD comes,
that great and terrible day.

The Spirit poured out on all people

32Then all who call on the name of the LORD will be saved.
On Mount Zion and in Jerusalem some will escape, as the LORD has said,
among the survivors
whom the LORD calls.
fields.summary: The day of God is coming like an army, so the people must return to God with all their heart. God will pity the people and restore what the locusts ate. God will pour out the Spirit on all people, sons and daughters, old and young, before the great day of God, and everyone who calls on the name of God will be rescued.

fields.title: Joel 3
fields.body_html:
1For in those days and at that time,
when I restore the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem,
2I will gather all the nations
and bring them down
into the valley of Jehoshaphat.
There I will bring them to judgment on behalf of my people, my inheritance Israel, whom they scattered among the nations,
and because they divided up my land.
3They cast lots for my people.
They traded boys for prostitutes
and sold girls for wine to drink.
4What are you to me, Tyre and Sidon
and all you regions of Philistia?
Are you paying me back for something?
If you are paying me back,
swiftly and speedily
I will turn your deeds back on your own heads.
5You took my silver and my gold,
and carried off my finest treasures
into your temples.
6You sold the people of Judah and of Jerusalem to the Greeks,
to send them far away from their own land.
7But now I am stirring them up
to leave the place
where you sold them,
and I will turn your deeds back on your own heads.

The nations judged in the valley of Jehoshaphat

8I will sell your sons and daughters to the people of Judah,
who will sell them to the Sabeans, a distant nation.
The LORD has spoken.

9Announce this among the nations:
Prepare for holy war!
Rouse the warriors!
Let them come forward and march up,
all the fighting men.
10Hammer your plow blades into swords
and your knives for pruning into spears.
Let the weakling say,
“I am a warrior!”
11Come quickly, all you nations on every side, and gather together!
Bring down your warriors there, LORD!
12Let the nations stir themselves and come up
to the valley of Jehoshaphat,
for there I will sit to judge all the surrounding nations.
13Swing the sickle,
for the harvest is ripe.
Come, tread the grapes, for the winepress is full.
The vats overflow,
because their wickedness is great.
14Crowds upon crowds
in the valley of decision!
Yes, the day of the LORD is close at hand
in the valley of decision.
15The sun and moon go dark,
and the stars lose their brightness.
16The LORD roars from Zion and thunders from Jerusalem,
and the heavens and the earth tremble.
But the LORD is a refuge for his people,
a fortress for the people of Israel.

A call to the nations to prepare for war

17Then you will know that I am the LORD your God,
living in Zion, my holy mountain.
Jerusalem will be holy,
and foreigners will never again march through it.

18On that day the mountains will drip sweet wine, and milk will flow from the hills;
all the streambeds of Judah will run with water.
A spring will flow out from the house of the LORD
and water the valley of Shittim.
19Egypt will be laid waste,
and Edom
will become a desolate wilderness,
because of the violence done to the people of Judah,
whose innocent blood they shed in their land.
20But Judah will be inhabited forever,
and Jerusalem for all generations.

Streams in Judah, and the LORD dwells in Zion

21I will avenge their blood, which I had left unavenged.
The LORD dwells in Zion.
fields.summary: God will gather the nations in the valley of Jehoshaphat to judge them for what they did to Judah. God roars from Zion and will dwell there, and Judah will be inhabited forever.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
I will avenge their blood, which I had left unavenged. The LORD dwells in Zion.

— Joel 3:21

Joel ends where it began, with God and his people and the land. The book opened on a temple with no offerings and a people in sackcloth. It closes with a spring flowing from the house of the LORD, and with the plainest promise a prophet can make: God is here, and he is staying.

The question the book leaves with you

Joel never explains why the locusts came. He does not list the people’s sins, as Amos and Hosea do. What he asks is what they will do now, in the ruins, and he answers for them: turn back to the LORD with all your heart. His “Yet even now” is the hinge of the book. However late it is, however bare the land, it is not too late to return to a God who is “gracious and full of tender compassion”.

And the book asks whom we expect God to pour out his Spirit on. Joel’s answer, everyone, sons and daughters, old and young, servants as well, is the answer of Pentecost. The church began on the day Peter read Joel aloud and said that it was happening.

Where to go from here

  • On the Spirit poured out (Joel 2:28–29). A. B. Simpson’s The Holy Spirit, or Power from on High, with its chapter “The Holy Spirit in the Book of Joel”; A. W. Tozer’s sermon All with One Accord (Acts 2:1), on the praying church to which Joel’s promise came; and Robert Murray M’Cheyne’s The Cry for Revival (Psalm 85:6), which pleads that promise for his own congregation.
  • On calling on the name of the LORD (Joel 2:32). Charles H. Spurgeon’s A Simple Sermon for Seeking Souls, on Paul’s use of Joel’s words in Romans 10:13; and his reading for January 16 in The Cheque Book of the Bank of Faith.
  • On returning with the heart (Joel 2:12–13). Spurgeon’s reading for December 18 in Morning by Morning, and the chapter on repentance in R. A. Torrey’s What the Bible Teaches.
  • On the years the locust has eaten (Joel 2:25). Spurgeon’s reading for May 18 in The Cheque Book of the Bank of Faith.
  • On telling the next generation (Joel 1:3). Spurgeon’s reading for July 11 in Evening by Evening.
  • On Joel and the gospel. Augustine’s The City of God, book XVIII, chapter 30, where he sets Joel beside Micah and Jonah.

Then read the second chapter of Acts beside the second chapter of Joel, and hear the promise and its keeping side by side. Joel’s last word on the subject is the one Peter and Paul both made their own:

Then all who call on the name of the LORD will be saved. On Mount Zion and in Jerusalem some will escape, as the LORD has said, among the survivors whom the LORD calls.

— Joel 2:32
